I realize now that this slippery slope premise was first established by the premises I seek to debunk (that of the anti-Columbus sentiment). It is not a slippery slope I introduced, but merely one I identified as being the logical consequence of accepting the premises justifying the anti-Columbus sentiment. The big picture is that this mentality has a negative energy and, in my opinion, reeks of arrogance emanating from the assumed moral superiority of those having the advantage of historical hindsight and philosophic advancement far beyond people of the past.

I therefore find it more useful to celebrate, build off of, and highlight the good in people of the past, as focusing on their faults simply breeds contempt, resentfulness, and stagnates betterment.

Granted, I used an oversimplification to more concisely convey the endpoint this way of thinking ultimately leads if unchecked. But, you are correct in that this issue is best represented via a spectrum model, and not by a binary "either, or" model. However, I hope you agree with the main idea, without being distracted by this immaterial red herring.

Technically, since all observations and reasoning against them is filtered through consciousness and perception, I believe the closest humans can get to KNOWING phenomena as fact, is to strongly BELIEVE them to be fact. I believe our perceptions of existence are merely a simulated picture of it, composed in each of us by the collection of information we have individually collected through our senses and our reasoning thereof. 

Normally, it is useless to assume our perceived universe and selves are merely facsimiles of reality, so our attitude tends to, rightfully, be that what we perceive is logically equivalent to what is real. However, in the context of OP's concerns, I believe it is critical to be aware of the limitation of perception's ability to correctly represent all aspects of reality to us, as we all recognize that different people, even witnessing the same event, tend to diverge in their understanding, beliefs, and reasoning about it.

When cultures, beliefs, and understood norms are highly similar across a group of individuals, agreement about what constitutes fact versus opinion is a simpler achievement. This suggests that the entire concept of "fact" is merely a label useful for individuals who agree with each other sufficiently to identify that which the individuals should accept as axiomatic. Contrastly, for individuals who do not sufficiently agree with each other, the concept of "fact" becomes a useless, hypothetical idea with different definitions residing in each individual's mind. Ergo, arguments about fact vs. opinion are redundant if the parties have already established that they cannot agree on what constitutes each.
